Roadmap to $10,000From Richard Ladson · working document

Some ideas for the business in your head

(Nothing here is decided. Tell me where I've got it wrong.)

For Sherene Woolcock

$10,000 a month, 20 hours a week.

Ideas for a business that pays you $10,000 a month for doing what you love, reaches far more families than you can today, and fits inside 20 hours a week.

Hi Sherene. When we talked, you said the number, and I heard four other things underneath it: you'd like a life you still get to enjoy, so this can't become a second full-time job; you've had a business in your head for years, you're on a mission to serve, and you'd rather never think about pricing, websites or software again. I put this together to show you how I'd build it with you, and to walk you through the process I use for every business, with yours as the example. If you only read one page, read this one.

The cliff notes

You already have the two hardest things a business needs: the expertise, and people who come to you for it. What's missing is structure, pricing and machinery, which are the easy things for me and the things you don't want. I'm suggesting you build your business, I build mine, and we work together on the projects that make sense for both: you do the care and the teaching, I do the business and the technology, the families who can't pay still get help, and the families who can pay are what make that possible. The $10,000 is the measure that it's working, and 20 hours a week is the limit that keeps it a life and not a second job.

How I'd like to use our time

What's in it for you, in four pages. Your story. The process I use. Your ideas, organized as I heard them. The messaging and the products it produces. What a family looks like when the software hands one to you. How we'd work together. What I still need to confirm with you. Then a small first step.

What I'm proposing

  • Write down the way you already work with families as a roadmap with a name at every step.
  • Build the products and the pricing around it, in versions for families who need care now and families planning ahead, with a free front door that never turns anyone away.
  • I build and run the websites, the software, the funnels and the follow-up; you never touch them.
  • We work out together what it takes to reach $10,000 a month, with real numbers, after you've corrected all of this.

What I'm not promising

  • An income. Nothing here is a projection until we build the scenarios together.
  • That any of this is right. It's my read of your work from my notes, and you correct it.
  • Clinical anything. The framework organizes; you and the family's clinicians decide.
  • That you'd stop helping people for free. That part stays. The structure is what lets it continue.

What I know about youWhat you told me, and what I noticed

What you told me, and what I noticed.

I'm starting from your words and what I've watched you do, not from a template.

Your goal

$10,000 a month

On top of what you do now. Not by finding more hours; you don't have them.

Your mission

To serve

Seniors and the families around them. You've held support groups for caregivers. You help people for free because that's who you are.

Your expertise

Memory care

Alzheimer's and dementia. Care plans, managing caregivers, what a good day looks like and what a bad night means. Plus the management experience to run it.

What I noticed

What you have

  • Ideas for a business you've carried for years.
  • Families already coming to you. That's demand, and it's the hardest thing to build.
  • A community you've already built, one support group at a time.
  • Your own story, with your father and your mother.

What's in the way

  • No framework for the business, so every family starts from scratch and you're the only one who can help.
  • No pricing, so the help is free by default, and free doesn't scale or fund itself.
  • The business side, websites and software: work you don't enjoy and shouldn't have to do.

What I believe

The problem was never generosity. It's that generosity without structure can't reach more than one family at a time and can't pay for itself. Structure is how you help more people, not fewer. That's the whole idea, and the rest of this deck is me showing my work.

Your storyThe reason families will trust you before they read a word

Your story is the front door.

Every family that finds you will want to know one thing before they read a checklist: does she understand what this is like? You do, and not from a textbook.

What I'd tell them, in your words, with your permission

You cared for your father. You've cared for your mother. You've sat in the chair the daughter with the stove is sitting in, and you've run the support groups where caregivers say out loud what they can't say at home. Then you spent a career learning how care actually gets organized, delivered and managed. There is no one else with both halves of that.

Why it matters to the business

  • Trust before the first call. A family chooses a guide they believe has walked the road. Your story does that work before you spend a minute.
  • The support groups you've hosted are already a product. In the model I work from, the ongoing community is the center of the business; everything else leads into it or grows out of it. You've built that center before, for free. It can be built again, with a structure that lets it last.
  • The mission stays visible. When the business is built around your story, pricing looks like what it is: the way the work keeps going.

The rule

Nothing about your family appears on a website, in an ad, or in a course until you've written it yourself and said yes. This page is a placeholder for your words, not mine.

The processWhat I do for every business I consider

The process I go through before I believe a number.

I've done this for my own practice and I'd like to do it with you, by hand, so you can see each step produce the next.

  1. Fix the transformation. One sentence: who you help, from what, to what. Then three phases and three steps in each. The roadmap has to be stable before anything is built on it.
  2. Name what you teach. Every step has three topics. Each gets a short name, a course title and a question a family would type into a search box.
  3. Say who it's for and what it produces. For each topic: the outcome, the three struggles, the three questions, the three actions, and the document the family walks away with.
  4. Split it into two versions. Families who need care now and families planning ahead do different work at the same step. Not softer wording; different checklists and different completion.
  5. Write the messaging. One message per topic in a fixed structure, and one educational ad that leads to one real thing.
  6. Package the products. Lead magnets at the front door, courses for self-study, guided and high-touch services above them, the community at the center, support after the handoff.
  7. Run the numbers. Only now: which products, at what capacity, reach the goal, and what has to be true for that to hold.

Why you can take this seriously

I've done every step of it for my own practice: my Medicaid Planning Roadmap, the software that produces the reports, the attorney relationship built the same way, and this deck. If you'd like to see what I did for my own business, I'd love to show you. Pages 9 to 21 are steps 1 through 6 done in draft for you. Step 7 is a meeting we have after you've torn this up and corrected it.

1 · The problemWhat's in it for you

You've been doing two jobs, and only one of them is yours.

The story

It's a Tuesday. A woman from church stops you after the service. Her mother left the stove on again, and could you talk for a minute. The minute is forty. By the end she understands her mother's situation better than she has in a year, she's crying a little, and she says she doesn't know how to thank you. You tell her not to worry about it. You mean it.

That night you think, again, about the business you've wanted to start. Then you think about the website, and the pricing, and the part where you'd have to ask that woman for money, and you go to bed.

The metaphor

You've been carrying two jobs. The first is the one you're brilliant at: understanding a person, building the plan, running the care, holding the room when caregivers finally say what they can't say at home. The second is the one you hate: the model, the prices, the website, the software, the follow-up. The second job has been sitting on top of the first for years, and it's the reason the first one has stayed the size of your calendar.

The model

Today

  • Help is free by default, because there's no structure to charge inside.
  • Every family starts from scratch, and only you can help.
  • The business side never gets built, because it's the part you'd never choose to do.
  • $10,000 a month would mean finding hours you don't have, and you've already said 20 a week is the most you'll give this.

With the second job taken off you

  • A free front door that never turns a family away, and paid tiers that fund it.
  • Every family starts from the same nine steps, and much of the work is done before they reach you.
  • The websites, software, funnels and follow-up are built and run by someone who likes that work.
  • $10,000 a month becomes a question of which families on which rungs.
2 · Your ideas, organizedWhat's in it for you

What if a family could follow your thinking without you in the room?

You described a lot in our conversation. What I've tried to do here is put it in an order a family could follow, so they can see where they are and what comes next. Tell me where I've got it wrong.

What I heard you say (in my words, so correct me)

  • Before anyone talks about facilities or caregivers, someone has to understand the person: what they can still do, what's changed, what a good day and a bad night look like.
  • Families are exhausted and guilty, and most of them are deciding in a crisis. The caregiver needs care too, and the support group is where that happens.
  • Home is the goal for as long as it's safe, and "safe" is something you can actually assess and revisit, not a feeling.
  • Care is a plan, then a team, then a routine. Managing the caregivers is most of the work, and nobody teaches families how.
  • A move to a facility, when it comes, should be a process the family leads with information, not an event that happens to them.
  • The family should end up able to run this themselves, with you a call away, not dependent on you forever.

When you talk about care, there's an order in it: understand the person, then work out what good care looks like, then run it and hand it back to the family. Those are the three rows. Three steps in each, all of it from what you said. It's a starting point, not a finished thing, and the names on the steps are the first thing I'd expect you to change.

The metaphor

A hymnal doesn't write the hymns. It puts them in an order a congregation can sing together, gives each one a number so people can find it, and lets a newcomer join in on the first Sunday. That's all a framework does to your ideas: an order, a name for every step, and a way for a family who's never met you to follow along.

Why write it down at all

You already know what a family should do first, second and third. Writing it down as nine steps means a family who hasn't met you yet can follow the same path, and it gives you:

  • A name for every step, so a family can say where they are and what comes next.
  • An order, so nobody tours facilities before they know what the person needs.
  • A deliverable, so every step ends with something in the family's hands, and something you can be paid for.
  • Two versions, so the woman with the stove and the son planning five years out both have a place to start.

The ideas are yours. If this way of organizing them doesn't fit how you think about care, we change the grid, not your ideas.

What you'd get, and what you'd stop doing.

4 · The benefitWhat's in it for you

More families, the same mission, and it pays you.

The story, again

Same Tuesday, a year from now. The woman from church doesn't have to catch you after the service. Her cousin sent her your checklist, "The First Care Conversation," and she answered the care interview that night. By morning she has a Family Care Profile that names the things only you can settle, and a button to book you. She joins the support group, which is back, with a name, a rhythm, and a way for people who can afford it to pay for it, so it never has to end. When she reaches you, the file is open and the forty minutes go to the part only you can do.

She pays for that part. Her neighbor, who can't, still gets the checklist, the interview and the group. Both of them got you.

The ladder

Front doorChecklists, guides, the care interviewFree, always. Finds the family before the crisis and never turns one away.
Self-directedThe mini-courses and worksheetsThe family learns the process. Your expertise, at scale.
The communityA support group, with structureThe center. What people stay for. Free and paid seats, agreed by you.
GuidedGroup coaching, office hours, reviewYou teach and review; you don't carry the file.
High-touchYou lead the coordinationDiscovery, assessment within scope, the plan, the transition, the handoff.

The benefit, plainly

  • Impact: more families reached than your calendar allows, and the free help continues because something funds it.
  • Income: $10,000 a month stops being "how many more families can I fit" and becomes "how many families on which rungs." That's a question with an answer, and we'll answer it together.
  • Relief: the second job is gone. You do the care, the teaching, and the room.

The line I'll keep

None of this asks you to make a clinical call you wouldn't make today, or to touch a family's money. The framework organizes and prepares; you and the family's clinicians decide. And the number stays a question until we build the scenarios together.

Your framework · two versionsNeed care now · Plan ahead

Two Versions of Every Step

The same nine steps, done differently depending on whether the family is in the middle of it or ahead of it. Not softer wording: different work, different completion.

Need Care Now

Care decisions, a transition, care-delivery concerns, or caregiver overload need attention now.

Understand the needs. Organize the plan. Coordinate the care.

Sherene helps families whose loved one needs care now understand the situation, organize a person-centered plan, and coordinate what happens next—without having to start every conversation from scratch, carry every task alone, or enter care meetings unprepared, even if the family is overwhelmed or unsure where to begin.

Plan Ahead

The family has time to document preferences, discuss roles, explore options, and prepare for changes.

Start the conversation. Prepare the family. Know when to act.

Sherene helps families prepare for an aging loved one’s changing care needs by documenting what matters, organizing a practical care roadmap, and preparing family roles and handoffs—without waiting for a crisis to start the conversation, assuming one person will handle everything, or making a placement decision before it is needed, even if their loved one is still largely independent.

Your framework · the lineWhat you do · what you never do

Where the Line Is

The framework organizes care information and prepares the family. It does not replace a clinician's plan, and it does not touch money. I wrote these from your boundaries as I understand them; correct me.

What you do

  • Care discovery, and assessment within your confirmed scope.
  • Care-plan preparation and provider-comparison support.
  • Transition coordination and care-plan meetings.
  • Family education, advocacy, and a practiced handoff.
  • Optional support after the handoff.

What you never do

  • Funding, Medi-Cal eligibility, insurance-funding or asset planning. That's my side.
  • Diagnose, prescribe, change medication, set clinical thresholds, or replace a provider's clinical plan.
  • Treat a relative's wishes as the person's own, or make activity attendance compulsory.
  • Call a course completion proof of a safe placement or a guaranteed result.

Still to confirm with you

Sherene’s credentials, included meetings, service area, support cadence, response expectations, and directory/data access remain to be confirmed. No prices or financial projections are included.

Your messagingStep 5 of the process

One structure, fifty-four messages.

Every topic gets three names and one message in a fixed shape, so the whole catalog speaks in one voice. Here's the structure, and one real example: Care Needs, the topic closest to what you do.

The message structure

[Topic] helps [specific families] achieve [outcome], without [struggle 1], [struggle 2] or [struggle 3], even if [objection].

No deadline, no guaranteed outcome, nothing a clinician or a provider controls.

The message, for Care Needs (need care now)

Care Needs helps families responding to a recent decline or care transition prepare a clear assessment summary of current functioning and questions for professional review, without guessing from a diagnosis alone, overlooking help already being provided, or mistaking a family worksheet for a clinical assessment—even if their abilities have changed recently.

Your productsStep 6 of the process

Four tiers, one ladder, no prices yet.

The same expertise packaged at four levels of your involvement. The prices, and how many families on each rung reach $10,000 a month, are the conversation after this one.

High-touch: Sherene leads the coordination

Personal family discovery and assessment within scope; care-plan preparation; provider-comparison support; transition coordination; explicitly included care-plan meetings; a practiced family handoff. Number of meetings and ongoing monitoring are not assumed.

Guided: Sherene teaches and reviews

The family uses the same templates and courses with defined group coaching, office hours, or review support. Individual clinical questions are routed to the appropriate professional rather than answered by a generic group curriculum.

Self-directed: the family learns the process

Courses, checklists, prompts, worksheets, and planning templates. Community access may be an optional addition. Self-study does not replace a professional assessment or create an ongoing care-management relationship.

Continuity: support after the handoff

Optional scheduled check-ins, future meeting help, a moderated community, or periodic gatherings. Scope, cadence, coverage during absence, and response expectations must be agreed; no unlimited access is implied.

What every topic can be sold as

  • A checklist or guide, free: the front door. Every brief in the appendix has one.
  • A mini-course, four lessons and a worksheet the family completes: the self-directed tier.
  • A guided review of that worksheet: the guided tier.
  • The step itself, done with you: the high-touch tier, where the currency of the step is earned.

How you'd know it's working, without a clinical score

Responsibility coverageWhich active coordination tasks have a confirmed owner and backup?
Open follow-upHow many agreed follow-up items are open or past their agreed date?

SEAM 1 · Family → you

The care interview and the Family Care Profile

A family answers my care interview and receives the profile you just saw. You receive the professional copy. Your Discover and Assess steps start with the file already open, and the family arrives with a booking, not a cold call.

SEAM 2 · You → my step 2

Your Care Needs Profile feeds my roadmap

Your step 3 produces the Care Needs Profile. Five facts from it are what my Medicaid assessment reads: the care setting, the monthly cost, the memory condition, who is planning, and the expected date of a move. My roadmap picks up at Organize with the care question already answered.

WHAT STAYS SEPARATE

Two lanes, one family

You never touch the money; I never make a care determination. The family sees one coordinated process; each of us stays inside our own scope.

How we'd work togetherTwo businesses, and the projects we share

Two businesses, working together where it makes sense.

You'd build your business and I'd build mine, and we'd partner on particular projects: a class, a course, a package that includes your service. That only holds if both of us can say what we put in, what we get, and who owns what. The shape is below; the numbers are for our numbers meeting.

What you bring

  • The expertise: assessment within your scope, care plans, coordination, the handoff.
  • The content: the substance of every course and checklist, corrected and approved by you.
  • The community: the support groups you've hosted, the families who already trust you, and the group we'd start again together.
  • Your story, on your terms.

What I bring

  • The framework, the business model and the pricing strategy.
  • The software: the care interview, the profiles, booking, follow-up and the family file.
  • The websites, the funnels, the ads and the measurement.
  • The Medicaid side of the family, when they need it, without you having to touch it.

What we'd need to agree, project by project (blank on purpose)

QuestionMy starting positionAgreed
How you get paidFor every family you serve, at prices we set together. Families you bring yourself are entirely yours; I don't participate in that revenue. Families who reach you through my packages or my front door are ones we share, on a split we agree.
How I get paidFrom the front end and the machinery I build and run: the courses, the community structure and the funnels. And from the packages I sell at different levels, some of which would include your service; on those we share. Splits to be agreed, in writing, before anything is sold.
Who owns the framework and the contentYour name, your story and anything you write are yours, always. The software, my Medicaid roadmap and the process are mine. The Family Care Roadmap we build together belongs to both of us: if this ends, we each keep the right to use it, and neither of us has to ask the other. Written up properly before anything is sold.
Who owns the familiesA family can have a relationship with both of us: the care relationship is yours, and what they pay you for it is yours, wherever you practice. Some of the same families will also be my clients, for keeping their Medicaid in good standing, and that relationship stays with me. Where a family has both, both continue. The list and the data live in the software under the privacy rules already written.
Your timeThe care and the teaching, at a capacity you set. Nothing on the business side.
DecisionsYou decide anything clinical, anything about the care, and anything said in your name. I decide the machinery. Pricing we decide together.
If it endsYou keep your name, your story, your relationships and the right to use everything we made together, and I keep mine. We agree the rest now, while we like each other.

Why the column is blank

Because you should react to the framework before we talk terms, and because I'd rather you hear a starting position than a finished deal. Nothing here is final.

What I need to confirm with youThe agenda for our next conversation

Everything in this deck rests on my notes. Here's what only you can settle.

Your credentials and scopeWhat assessment you are licensed or trained to do, so every page says 'within scope' truthfully.
The high-touch engagementWhat it includes: how many meetings, whether ongoing monitoring is in, what a handoff looks like.
Where you serveCounties, in person or remote, and the response time a family can expect.
Provider accessWhich communities and agencies you can compare, and what records you can see.
The two versionsWhether the need-care-now and plan-ahead split matches how families actually reach you.
The clinical notesHydration, infections, medication review, food texture and skin care appear in the briefs as topics for a professional, never as instructions. Tell me if any of it is wrong.
Your name on itWhether you want the roadmap in your name, and what you'd call it.

The rule I'll keep

Nothing here becomes a product until you've corrected it. The briefs in the appendix are marked 'Sherene review pending' on every page for that reason.

The numbers come nextStep 7 of the process

The path to $10,000 a month in 20 hours a week is a set of scenarios, not a promise.

Once you've reacted to the framework and the products, we build the numbers together, and they'll only be as honest as the inputs you give me. One input is already fixed: 20 hours a week, and every scenario has to fit inside it.

  • Your capacity: 20 hours a week, split between the high-touch families you carry, the guided sessions you lead and a support group, if we bring one back. The split is yours; the total isn't negotiable.
  • Your prices: what each rung costs, set by you, informed by what the deliverable at that step is worth to a family.
  • The mix: how many families on which rungs, and how the front door feeds them.
  • What has to be true: the front-door volume, the conversion from checklist to interview to booking, and the months it takes.

Why 20 hours changes the shape of the business

If every dollar came from your hours, $10,000 in 80 hours a month is $125 an hour, every hour, with no gaps and no free help. That's a job, not the business you described. The courses, the community and the front door are what earn while you're not in the room, and they're what makes the number possible at 20 hours instead of 50.

What I'll bring

The front-door numbers from my side, the interview and the profile, are measurable from day one; my software records every step a family takes. What I can't bring is your capacity and your prices. That's the meeting.

What I won't do

Put a projection in front of you before we've done that. The $10,000 in this deck is your number and your ceiling of 20 hours, not my forecast.

The riskThe part I'd rather say now than in month four

I should be candid: this might not work.

Most businesses fail. This one could too, and I'd rather put that on a page now than have you find it out four months in.

How it could fail

  • The money runs out. I'm putting up the capital to get this started. If the ads cost more than the families they bring in, or it takes longer than I've planned, I could run out before it works.
  • Families don't buy. They may love the free help and never pay for the rest. Or we price it wrong, in either direction, and find out slowly.
  • The front door doesn't fill. The checklist doesn't get downloaded, the interview doesn't get finished, the room stays empty. I've built the machinery, not the guarantee that people walk through it.
  • We don't teach well together, or you find you don't enjoy it. That's exactly what the one class is for, but it's a real possibility.
  • Life happens. One of us gets sick, or gets pulled back to family, or a Medicaid rule changes under us, or someone bigger shows up with a better version.
  • Something I haven't thought of. That's usually the one.

What that means for the number

There's no guarantee you'll make $10,000 a month, or $1. The same is true for me. We could build all of this, launch it, have nobody buy, and end up broke with nothing to show for it but egg on our faces and a lesson in how not to do it. That's the risk, and it's real.

What I can promise

  • I'm giving it my best shot, and I'm putting everything I have into it.
  • I'm committed to supporting you and helping you reach your goals, to the best of my ability.
  • If it doesn't work, and it may not, we'll have a good story to tell.
  • If, by the grace of God, it does work, I'll treat you fairly, and I'll think win-win in every decision I make.
  • I'll be honest with you and act with integrity: I'll say what I mean, I'll mean what I say, and I'll do what I say I'm going to do.

What I can't promise

  • That it works.
  • An income, for you or for me.
  • How long it takes.
  • That my plan survives contact with real families. It won't, entirely, and we'll change it as we go.
The askA first step small enough to say yes to

What I'm asking for today.

Not a business partnership, and not a decision about anything. Three small things, in order, and each one tells us whether the next one makes sense.

  1. Read your framework and correct it. Pages 9 to 17. Tell me what's wrong, what's missing, and what you'd never say. Your credentials and scope first, because everything rests on them.
  2. Teach one class with me, online. A single webinar, sixty to ninety minutes, on one topic from your framework, for families I bring. Your part would be to review the material (or write it, if you'd rather; either way it's yours), teach it alongside me, and answer the questions at the end. I'd build everything else and fill the room. It tells us three things nothing else can: whether we teach well together, whether families show up, and whether you enjoy it. Is that something you could do?
  3. Have the numbers meeting. With the class behind us: how you'd spend the 20 hours, your prices, the mix of families on each rung, and what has to be true to reach $10,000 a month inside them. Then we decide whether to write the terms.

What you'd be committing to

An afternoon with the framework, and one evening teaching with me, plus an hour or two to look over the material. Nothing else until you've seen it work.

What I'm committing to

To build and run every piece of the machinery for the class at my cost, to fill the room, to change anything you say is wrong, and to keep your name off anything until you've approved it.

Appendix A · BoundariesFrom the package

Boundaries

Service scopeSherene’s working lane is care discovery, assessment within confirmed scope, planning support, coordination, family education, advocacy, and handoff. Funding, Medicaid eligibility, insurance-funding, and asset planning are excluded.
Professional rolesThe curriculum organizes care information and prepares questions. It does not authorize families or AI to diagnose, prescribe, change medication, set clinical thresholds, or replace a provider’s clinical plan.
Person-centered careThe loved one’s stated preferences remain separate from family wishes. Activity support should preserve choice rather than require attendance.
Draft versus deliveryCourse completion produces an organized learner output. It is not proof of safe placement, a guaranteed care result, or confirmation that Sherene has accepted a professional engagement.
Unknowns and evidenceProvider availability, capabilities, information access, and the actual care-plan review schedule require case-specific confirmation. Missing evidence is not an on-plan status.
Unconfirmed business detailsSherene’s credentials, included meetings, service area, support cadence, response expectations, and directory/data access remain to be confirmed. No prices or financial projections are included.
Advertising statusAds are draft copy. No assertion is made about current ad-platform eligibility, approved targeting, conversion rates, or a live landing page. Claims and destinations need review before launch.
Appendix B · Service tiersFrom the package

Service tiers

High-touch: Sherene leads the coordinationPersonal family discovery and assessment within scope; care-plan preparation; provider-comparison support; transition coordination; explicitly included care-plan meetings; a practiced family handoff. Number of meetings and ongoing monitoring are not assumed.
Guided: Sherene teaches and reviewsThe family uses the same templates and courses with defined group coaching, office hours, or review support. Individual clinical questions are routed to the appropriate professional rather than answered by a generic group curriculum.
Self-directed: the family learns the processCourses, checklists, prompts, worksheets, and planning templates. Community access may be an optional addition. Self-study does not replace a professional assessment or create an ongoing care-management relationship.
Continuity: support after the handoffOptional scheduled check-ins, future meeting help, a moderated community, or periodic gatherings. Scope, cadence, coverage during absence, and response expectations must be agreed; no unlimited access is implied.
Appendix C · MetricsProposed, non-clinical

Proposed non-clinical metrics

MeasureQuestionHow it is recorded
Responsibility coverageWhich active coordination tasks have a confirmed owner and backup?Task table; confirmation date; not a clinical-quality score.
Open follow-upHow many agreed follow-up items are open or past their agreed date?Open, waiting, overdue, resolved; retain the source of the date.
Handoff completionWhich transfers have a recorded recipient acknowledgment?Sent, received, needs clarification, resolved.
Information freshnessWhen was the family plan or contact list last reviewed?Document version and last-reviewed date; no universal review interval assumed.
Caregiver capacityDoes the lead caregiver report that current responsibilities are manageable?A conversation prompt and agreed action, not a diagnostic burnout score.
Person’s experienceWhat does the person report about routines, choices, and meaningful activities?Use their words where possible; record offers and support without rewarding forced participation.
Care-plan follow-throughWhat is known about a small set of agreed care-plan items?Observed, reported, unknown, or needs follow-up, with source and date; clinical interpretation remains with professionals.

4 · Three struggles

  • Repeating the same story to different people.
  • Relying on scattered notes.

5 · Three questions

  • What has changed?
  • Who is coordinating care right now?
  • What decision must our family make next?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Care Situation helps families facing an urgent care decision create one clear summary of the current care situation and the next decisions, without repeating the same story to different people, relying on scattered notes, or assuming someone else is handling an important task—even if nobody has organized the information before.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineCare Decisions Are Urgent. Where Do You Start?
Primary textA care transition can bring several conversations at once: family, caregivers, and the care team. Start by putting the situation in one place. Organize what has happened, who is involved, and the decisions your family faces next.
BenefitGet a clearer starting point for the next care conversation.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe First Care Conversation Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Record the event or change that created the immediate need.
  2. Confirm upcoming care decisions and any stated dates.
  3. Name a temporary family contact and a backup.

Working actions

  1. Document where the person lives and who provides help.
  2. Describe morning, daytime, evening, and overnight arrangements.
  3. List family members, professionals, and contact details.
  4. Record what each person actually does.
  5. Ask the primary caregiver which responsibilities are becoming difficult.
  6. Gather relevant existing care notes with appropriate permission.
  7. Separate confirmed facts, family observations, and unanswered questions.
  8. Review the summary with the loved one where possible and with the family.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The family and Sherene have a current summary, an identified contact, and a list of immediate decisions with unknowns clearly marked.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Start with the immediate decision
    • What triggered the request for help.
    • Which decision is next.
    • Who needs the situation summary today.
  2. Lesson 2 · Describe the situation
    • Separate current arrangements from proposed changes.
    • Describe a typical day rather than relying on broad labels.
    • Record what changed and when.
  3. Lesson 3 · Map the people and work
    • List family and professional caregivers.
    • Compare actual workload with assumed responsibilities.
    • Identify the person coordinating information.
  4. Lesson 4 · Build the starting summary
    • Combine notes without erasing disagreement.
    • Mark unknown information rather than filling gaps.
    • Prepare a focused review with Sherene.

11 · The deliverable the family completes

TitleFamily Care Situation Summary
PurposeCreate one clear summary of the current care situation and the next decisions.

Fields:

  • Reason for seeking help
  • Current living and care arrangement
  • Typical day
  • People involved and their actual tasks
  • Recent changes and upcoming decisions
  • Information still missing
  • Next conversation and its owner

Blank learner-output specification; not a completed assessment or plan for an actual family.

14 · Prompt guide

5 AI Prompts for Care Situation — Need Care Now

Use only de-identified information you have permission to share. Treat AI as an organizer and drafting assistant, not as a clinician, a safety assessor, or a decision-maker for the person. Preserve unknowns, disagreements, and sources. Do not invent diagnoses, care orders, medication changes, clinical thresholds, provider capabilities, or legal authority. Flag decisions for the appropriate human professional. Do not use a prompt, course, or community channel as an urgent-help service.

  1. We need to address an active care situation now. Using only these notes [paste de-identified notes], help me organize our notes into a current-situation summary with a typical-day section. Mark missing information and decisions requiring human review. Give me an editable draft, not a clinical conclusion.
  2. We need to address an active care situation now. Using only these notes [paste de-identified notes], help me create an interview agenda that lets our loved one and the main caregiver speak. Mark missing information and decisions requiring human review. Give me an editable draft, not a clinical conclusion.
  3. We need to address an active care situation now. Using only these notes [paste de-identified notes], help me turn a list of caregiving tasks into a who-does-what table without assigning unwilling relatives. Mark missing information and decisions requiring human review. Give me an editable draft, not a clinical conclusion.
  4. We need to address an active care situation now. Using only these notes [paste de-identified notes], help me identify gaps or contradictions in the information without guessing which account is correct. Mark missing information and decisions requiring human review. Give me an editable draft, not a clinical conclusion.
  5. We need to address an active care situation now. Using only these notes [paste de-identified notes], help me draft a concise briefing for Sherene that distinguishes known facts from questions. Mark missing information and decisions requiring human review. Give me an editable draft, not a clinical conclusion.

  • What help is already being provided?
  • Who knows our loved one’s daily routine?
  • What information should we organize while there is time?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Care Situation helps families preparing for an aging loved one’s changing needs document the current care arrangement and establish a starting point for future decisions, without waiting for a crisis to compare notes, assuming relatives understand the same situation, or leaving everyday caregiving work invisible—even if your loved one is still largely independent.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Invite the loved one to describe an ordinary week.
  2. List existing help and informal caregiving.
  3. Agree when the family will revisit the summary.

Working actions

  1. Document where the person lives and who provides help.
  2. Describe morning, daytime, evening, and overnight arrangements.
  3. List family members, professionals, and contact details.
  4. Record what each person actually does.
  5. Ask the primary caregiver which responsibilities are becoming difficult.
  6. Gather relevant existing care notes with appropriate permission.
  7. Separate confirmed facts, family observations, and unanswered questions.
  8. Review the summary with the loved one where possible and with the family.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

A current care summary exists, the family knows where it is kept, and a review date or change trigger has been identified.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Begin before decisions become urgent
    • Invite participation rather than announce a decision.
    • Document existing help.
    • Set a sensible reason to review the picture again.
  2. Lesson 2 · Describe the situation
    • Separate current arrangements from proposed changes.
    • Describe a typical day rather than relying on broad labels.
    • Record what changed and when.
  3. Lesson 3 · Map the people and work
    • List family and professional caregivers.
    • Compare actual workload with assumed responsibilities.
    • Identify the person coordinating information.
  4. Lesson 4 · Build the starting summary
    • Combine notes without erasing disagreement.
    • Mark unknown information rather than filling gaps.
    • Prepare a focused review with Sherene.

4 · Three struggles

  • Trying to solve every disagreement at once.
  • Turning concerns into personal accusations.
  • Overlooking the caregiver who is running out of capacity.

5 · Three questions

  • What is actually going wrong?
  • Which responsibilities are not getting done?
  • What help does the primary caregiver need now?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Care Challenges helps families dealing with care breakdowns or caregiver overwhelm identify the care problems that need attention and organize the conversations needed to address them, without trying to solve every disagreement at once, turning concerns into personal accusations, or overlooking the caregiver who is running out of capacity—even if the family does not agree on the cause of the problem.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineToo Many Care Problems at Once?
Primary textA missed task, an overwhelmed caregiver, and an argument between siblings are different problems. A clear issue list helps the family discuss each one more constructively. Sort care concerns, family disagreements, and caregiver overload into a focused list of next actions.

StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. List current care gaps and upcoming decisions.
  2. Ask the primary caregiver what must change immediately.
  3. Identify concerns that need prompt attention from the responsible care professional.

Working actions

  1. Invite the loved one and family to name their main concerns.
  2. Write a concrete example for each concern.
  3. Record whether care, communication, paperwork, or workload is involved.
  4. Ask the lead caregiver which tasks cannot continue as they are.
  5. Document differing accounts without declaring a winner.
  6. Identify unresolved concerns needing professional attention.
  7. Select the concerns to discuss in the next family meeting.
  8. Assign a next action and follow-up owner for each selected issue.
  9. Keep an open-issues list rather than expecting one meeting to resolve everything.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The main concerns are documented with examples, caregiver capacity is visible, and each immediate issue has a next contact or action.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Focus the next conversation
    • Name the active problem.
    • Recognize overloaded caregivers.
    • Keep the discussion centered on the loved one’s needs.
  2. Lesson 2 · Name the actual problem
    • Replace broad complaints with specific examples.
    • Distinguish observations from interpretations.
    • Ask how the concern affects daily care.
  3. Lesson 3 · Include the caregiver and family
    • Make hidden workload visible.
    • Discuss unkept commitments without labeling relatives.
    • Notice conflict over a move or increased support.
  4. Lesson 4 · Prepare a useful conversation
    • Group related concerns.
    • State what needs clarification or help.
    • Refer concerns outside the service’s scope to the appropriate professional.

6 · Million Dollar Message

Family Priorities helps families making a difficult care decision create shared decision criteria while keeping the loved one’s wishes and unresolved disagreements visible, without assuming everyone wants the same outcome, letting the loudest voice define the plan, or losing the person’s preferences in a rushed decision—even if you cannot reach complete agreement today.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineHow Do You Choose When the Family Disagrees?
Primary textA difficult care decision is easier to discuss when the family can name what matters, what is disputed, and what still needs clarification. Start there rather than arguing over a solution. Bring your loved one’s wishes and the family’s concerns into the same care conversation.
BenefitPrepare a more focused family care conversation.
ActionClick below to learn more.

StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Ask for the loved one’s current preferences.
  2. Name the decision that needs to be made.
  3. Document shared priorities and unresolved differences before comparing solutions.

Working actions

  1. Ask the loved one what matters most to them.
  2. Record routines and choices they want preserved.
  3. Ask each involved family member about concerns and desired outcomes.
  4. Separate the person’s wishes from the family’s preferences.
  5. Document where expectations conflict.
  6. Discuss what relatives can and cannot realistically provide.
  7. List questions requiring clinical or other professional clarification.
  8. Agree on criteria to use when comparing care options.
  9. Review the profile with the person where possible.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The profile separates the person’s wishes from family preferences and records decision criteria, unresolved issues, and who will clarify them.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Use priorities in an active decision
    • Keep the person’s voice visible.
    • Do not require artificial consensus.
    • Identify the information needed to move forward.
  2. Lesson 2 · Listen to the person receiving care
    • Ask what makes a good day.
    • Capture their own words when possible.
    • Do not replace their preferences with family assumptions.
  3. Lesson 3 · Listen to the family
    • Explore hopes and worries.
    • Separate preferences from available caregiving capacity.
    • Identify competing expectations.
  4. Lesson 4 · Create shared decision criteria
    • Record agreement and disagreement.
    • Identify tradeoffs for discussion.
    • Keep unresolved issues visible in the planning file.

Primary textYou can talk about a good day, independence, and who should be involved without asking anyone to agree to a move. Those conversations can become the starting point for future planning. Learn what your loved one values and what the family hopes to preserve as care needs change.
BenefitStart the conversation about what matters most.
ActionClick below to learn more.

StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Ask permission to discuss future support.
  2. Begin with routines and preferences rather than a proposed move.
  3. Agree how preferences will be revisited as circumstances change.

Working actions

  1. Ask the loved one what matters most to them.
  2. Record routines and choices they want preserved.
  3. Ask each involved family member about concerns and desired outcomes.
  4. Separate the person’s wishes from the family’s preferences.
  5. Document where expectations conflict.
  6. Discuss what relatives can and cannot realistically provide.
  7. List questions requiring clinical or other professional clarification.
  8. Agree on criteria to use when comparing care options.
  9. Review the profile with the person where possible.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

Preferences and family priorities are documented, unanswered questions remain visible, and the family has agreed how to continue the conversation.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Start without forcing a decision
    • Ask permission.
    • Use everyday-life questions.
    • Treat the profile as something that can change.
  2. Lesson 2 · Listen to the person receiving care
    • Ask what makes a good day.
    • Capture their own words when possible.
    • Do not replace their preferences with family assumptions.
  3. Lesson 3 · Listen to the family
    • Explore hopes and worries.
    • Separate preferences from available caregiving capacity.
    • Identify competing expectations.
  4. Lesson 4 · Create shared decision criteria
    • Record agreement and disagreement.
    • Identify tradeoffs for discussion.
    • Keep unresolved issues visible in the planning file.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Obtain the latest available care and discharge information.
  2. Document present abilities rather than only pre-hospital abilities.
  3. List clinical questions that must be clarified for the next arrangement.

Working actions

  1. Invite the loved one to describe what they can do and where help is useful.
  2. Record assistance with daily activities.
  3. Describe mobility and transfer support currently used.
  4. Gather current care instructions and relevant records.
  5. Record cognitive, emotional, and communication observations.
  6. Compile medication-management questions without changing medications.
  7. Record nutrition, swallowing, continence, and skin concerns for review.
  8. List therapies or services already involved.
  9. Arrange Sherene’s review within her confirmed professional scope.
  10. Route unresolved clinical questions to the responsible clinician.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

Current abilities, assistance, information sources, and open clinical questions are documented and assigned for professional review.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Assess the current picture
    • Notice recent changes.
    • Use current information.
    • Clarify what is not yet known.
  2. Lesson 2 · Describe everyday function
    • Discuss bathing, dressing, eating, toileting, and moving.
    • Record what the person does independently.
    • Describe assistance without treating a checklist as a diagnosis.
  3. Lesson 3 · Organize health-related information
    • Collect existing care instructions and medication information.
    • Record cognitive, emotional, nutrition, and communication concerns.
    • List questions for the appropriate clinician.
  4. Lesson 4 · Prepare the professional assessment
    • Compare family reports with the person’s account.
    • Identify information Sherene needs to confirm.
    • Maintain a source and date for observations.

  • Assuming help will be available.

  • When will help be needed?
  • Who is actually available?

6 · Million Dollar Message

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineWill the Next Care Arrangement Have the Support It Needs?
Primary textA care plan needs more than a location. It also needs clear answers about assistance, supervision, backup coverage, and concerns that require professional review. Identify coverage gaps and questions the responsible professionals need to address before the arrangement changes.
BenefitReview the support questions before the next care transition.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe Care Support Readiness Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Map support for the proposed next arrangement.
  2. Identify unfilled help or supervision periods.
  3. Take unresolved safety questions to the responsible care professional.

Working actions

  1. Document observed fall or mobility concerns.
  2. List times when supervision or help may be unavailable.
  3. Record medication-management difficulties for review.
  4. Identify environmental concerns reported or observed.
  5. Review the primary caregiver’s ability to provide the agreed help.
  6. Record relevant existing professional instructions.
  7. Identify missing backup coverage.
  8. Ask the appropriate professional to review unresolved safety questions.
  9. Record owners and follow-up for proposed changes.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

Current concerns and coverage gaps are visible, each has an owner, and unresolved safety questions have been referred rather than treated as cleared.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Review the proposed arrangement
    • Compare support needed with support available.
    • Check handoffs and overnight arrangements.
    • Do not equate a completed worksheet with safety clearance.
  2. Lesson 2 · Observe the environment and support
    • Document specific concerns rather than certify a home safe.
    • Identify when the person is alone.
    • Describe assistance currently available.
  3. Lesson 3 · Review coverage and caregiver capacity
    • Map daytime and overnight coverage.
    • Identify backup arrangements.
    • Include the caregiver’s practical limits.
  4. Lesson 4 · Create a professional follow-up list
    • Use existing instructions as the starting point.
    • Route clinical questions to the care team.
    • Record who will follow up on each concern.

  6. Record relevant existing professional instructions.
  7. Identify missing backup coverage.
  8. Ask the appropriate professional to review unresolved safety questions.
  9. Record owners and follow-up for proposed changes.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

A support map, backup questions, and professional-review list exist, with an agreed reason to revisit them.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Review assumptions while there is time
    • Consider absences and changing availability.
    • Ask caregivers about capacity.
    • Plan to revisit the review after changes.
  2. Lesson 2 · Observe the environment and support
    • Document specific concerns rather than certify a home safe.
    • Identify when the person is alone.
    • Describe assistance currently available.
  3. Lesson 3 · Review coverage and caregiver capacity
    • Map daytime and overnight coverage.
    • Identify backup arrangements.
    • Include the caregiver’s practical limits.
  4. Lesson 4 · Create a professional follow-up list
    • Use existing instructions as the starting point.
    • Route clinical questions to the care team.
    • Record who will follow up on each concern.

CurrencyRecognition
OutcomeCreate an About Me profile that carries the person’s daily preferences into the new care relationship.

4 · Three struggles

  • Relying on relatives to repeat every detail.
  • Losing familiar routines during admission.
  • Substituting family wishes for the person’s own choices.

5 · Three questions

  • What should new caregivers know about the person?
  • Which routines help them feel comfortable?
  • How do we communicate preferences clearly?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Personal Preferences helps families introducing a loved one to new caregivers create an About Me profile that carries the person’s daily preferences into the new care relationship, without relying on relatives to repeat every detail, losing familiar routines during admission, or substituting family wishes for the person’s own choices—even if important details have never been written down.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineWill the Care Team Know More Than a Diagnosis?
Primary textMorning tea, familiar activities, and how someone likes to be approached belong in the care conversation. An About Me profile helps the family share those details clearly. Put meaningful routines, communication preferences, and daily choices into an easy-to-share profile.

ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe About Me Handoff Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Ask which routines matter most during this transition.
  2. Prepare a concise profile for new caregivers.
  3. Confirm who will receive and review it.

Working actions

  1. Ask the person to describe a good day.
  2. Record preferred morning and evening routines.
  3. Document meal preferences and usual timing.
  4. Keep allergies and clinician-prescribed dietary instructions distinct from preferences.
  5. List meaningful activities and relationships.
  6. Describe communication approaches the person prefers.
  7. Ask what helps during an unfamiliar situation.
  8. Confirm the profile with the person where possible.
  9. Prepare a short version for authorized care-team sharing.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

A person-centered profile is confirmed where possible, preferences are distinguished from care orders, and a sharing recipient is identified.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Introduce the person to new caregivers
    • Choose immediately useful details.
    • Keep the profile readable.
    • Ask the receiving team to confirm receipt.
  2. Lesson 2 · Learn the person’s ordinary day
    • Ask open-ended questions.
    • Use their own words where possible.
    • Include familiar routines and relationships.
  3. Lesson 3 · Capture preferences accurately
    • Separate wishes from clinical instructions.
    • Record what support participation requires.
    • Notice disagreement between family assumptions and the person’s preferences.
  4. Lesson 4 · Create the About Me profile
    • Keep the staff-facing version easy to read.
    • Confirm what the person wants shared.
    • Plan how preferences can be updated.

Find the Gaps in Today’s Care. Compare what your loved one needs with the help actually in place.

1 · Names

Short nameCare Gaps

General topicNeeds & Risks

2 · Currency · 3 · Outcome

CurrencyVisibility
OutcomeCreate a documented list of care gaps and the follow-up each one requires.

4 · Three struggles

  • Assuming a listed service is being delivered.
  • Confusing uncertainty with a confirmed failure.
  • Overlooking gaps covered informally by one exhausted relative.

5 · Three questions

  • Which needs are not being met?
  • What do we know and what still needs checking?
  • Who will address each gap?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Care Gaps helps families concerned that current care is not meeting identified needs create a documented list of care gaps and the follow-up each one requires, without assuming a listed service is being delivered, confusing uncertainty with a confirmed failure, or overlooking gaps covered informally by one exhausted relative—even if the available information is incomplete.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineWhat Is Falling Through the Cracks?
Primary textA useful care review compares the plan with the real arrangement. See which needs have support, which are uncertain, and which need a clear follow-up. Compare what your loved one needs with the help actually in place.
BenefitIdentify the gaps that need a care conversation.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe Care Gaps Review Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Compare current needs with actual daily support.
  2. Verify unclear information with the appropriate source.
  3. Assign prompt follow-up to unresolved concerns.

Working actions

  1. Gather the family summary and assessment findings.
  2. List each documented support need.
  3. Identify what currently meets that need.
  4. Flag needs with no reliable support.
  5. Record conflicting or missing information.
  6. Include meaningful-activity and communication gaps.
  7. Identify where family commitments exceed capacity.
  8. Refer clinical uncertainty for professional review.
  9. Assign a next step for each unresolved gap.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

Each identified gap has a source, an owner, a status, and a next action or professional-review route.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Review the active arrangement
    • Work from current observations.
    • Check assumptions.
    • Make follow-up ownership explicit.
  2. Lesson 2 · Bring the assessment together
    • Combine person, family, and professional information.
    • Retain sources and uncertainties.
    • Avoid treating repeated statements as independent confirmation.
  3. Lesson 3 · Compare needs with actual support
    • Identify assistance already in place.
    • Make uncovered tasks visible.
    • Include caregiver capacity and meaningful daily life.
  4. Lesson 4 · Create an actionable gap register
    • State gaps neutrally.
    • Assign professional-review questions.
    • Prepare priorities for the roadmap.

6 · Million Dollar Message

HeadlineWhat Must the Next Care Setting Be Able to Do?

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Confirm current requirements with the relevant care professionals.
  2. Identify capabilities needed in the next arrangement.
  3. Record questions that must be resolved before selection.

Working actions

  1. Review the completed needs and gaps register.
  2. List tasks needing assistance.
  3. Record timing or frequency only when documented or confirmed.
  4. Identify supervision questions needing assessment.
  5. List clinical capabilities the care team says are required.
  6. Document mobility and communication support.
  7. Confirm realistic family participation.
  8. Separate essential capabilities from preferences.
  9. Have the appropriate professional review unresolved care-level questions.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The brief identifies confirmed requirements, open clinical questions, and the capabilities providers must be asked to verify.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Define requirements for the next arrangement
    • Use current assessment findings.
    • Separate essentials from preferences.
    • Ask for confirmation rather than guessing.
  2. Lesson 2 · Describe required assistance
    • Translate observations into questions about support.
    • Include timing and availability.
    • Do not infer a formal eligibility determination.
  3. Lesson 3 · Identify essential capabilities
    • List supervision and professional-service requirements.
    • Distinguish confirmed requirements from open questions.
    • Consider the family’s practical contribution.
  4. Lesson 4 · Prepare for settings comparison
    • Write needs-based criteria.
    • Get professional confirmation where required.
    • Carry the brief into provider research.

4 · Three struggles

  • Trying to do everything at once.
  • Taking steps before their prerequisites are resolved.
  • Leaving one relative to coordinate every task.

5 · Three questions

  • What should happen first?
  • Who is responsible?
  • What must be clarified before we act?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Care Roadmap helps families facing several immediate care decisions create a prioritized care roadmap with clear responsibilities and professional follow-up, without trying to do everything at once, taking steps before their prerequisites are resolved, or leaving one relative to coordinate every task—even if you do not yet have every answer.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineWhat Should the Family Do Next?
Primary textKnowing the concerns is not the same as knowing the next step. A written roadmap shows what comes first, who will do it, and which questions still need professional input. Turn assessments and open questions into an organized sequence of care actions.
BenefitOrganize your family’s next care steps.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe Next Care Steps Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Identify the next decision and any confirmed deadline.
  2. Prioritize its prerequisites and professional questions.
  3. Assign owners and confirm what the lead caregiver can realistically handle.

Working actions

  1. Review assessment findings and unresolved questions.
  2. List decisions that need to be made.
  3. List actions needed before those decisions.
  4. Identify professional reviews and who will request them.
  5. Separate actions to do now, later, or when a trigger occurs.
  6. Assign a willing owner to each active task.
  7. Confirm backups for important responsibilities.
  8. Record agreed dates and dependencies.
  9. Check whether the primary caregiver’s workload is realistic.
  10. Share the roadmap with authorized participants.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The next actions are sequenced, owned, and dated where appropriate, and unresolved decisions have a clear review route.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Sequence urgent care work
    • Start with actual decision dates.
    • Identify prerequisites.
    • Do not let incomplete information disappear.
  2. Lesson 2 · Turn findings into actions
    • Translate concerns into specific next steps.
    • Distinguish decisions from tasks.
    • Keep professional-review items visible.
  3. Lesson 3 · Sequence the work
    • Identify dependencies.
    • Separate immediate action from monitoring.
    • Assign owners according to actual capacity.
  4. Lesson 4 · Create the shared roadmap
    • Record dates and follow-up.
    • Identify a backup for critical tasks.
    • Review the roadmap with participants.

  • Treating directory entries as current availability.

  • Can this provider address the documented requirements?
  • What is available now?
  • Which answers still need verification?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Provider Search helps families looking for a provider for an active care need create a verified research sheet showing which providers require further evaluation, without treating directory entries as current availability, assuming all shifts have the same staffing, or choosing from unverified claims or impressions—even if the search needs to move quickly.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineWhat Should You Ask Before Choosing a Provider?
Primary textAvailability is only one question. Families also need to ask about actual support, staffing coverage, daily routines, and the capabilities their loved one requires. Check capabilities, availability, and daily-care details instead of relying on a brochure alone.
BenefitGet the questions for a more focused provider search.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe Care Provider Interview Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Identify requirements that must be confirmed before admission or service start.
  2. Contact providers about current availability.
  3. Record unresolved capability questions for immediate follow-up.

Working actions

  1. Create search criteria from the care requirements brief.
  2. Identify relevant providers through available resources.
  3. Contact providers to confirm current availability.
  4. Ask about private and shared room arrangements.
  5. Ask which staff provide support during each shift.
  6. Clarify nursing availability and what happens when a need exceeds routine coverage.
  7. Ask about required mobility, communication, and personal-care support.
  8. Ask about activities and help to participate.
  9. Clarify therapy coordination and changing-care arrangements.
  10. Record the source and date for each answer.
  11. Record inspection or other quality information separately from provider claims.
  12. List questions to verify during a tour or follow-up.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

Provider records include current sources, dates, capability questions, and unresolved items; no unverified entry is treated as an accepted placement.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Research for an active need
    • Verify availability directly.
    • Prioritize essential capability questions.
    • Track who provided each answer.
  2. Lesson 2 · Build the search criteria
    • Use essential requirements and preferences.
    • Include location and family access.
    • Avoid collecting information with no decision purpose.
  3. Lesson 3 · Ask providers specific questions
    • Ask about current availability.
    • Distinguish daytime and overnight coverage.
    • Ask how the person’s particular support needs would be addressed.
  4. Lesson 4 · Verify and document the findings
    • Record the source and date.
    • Separate provider statements from independent information.
    • Keep unknowns visible rather than assigning an unsupported rank.

  • Source of quality information
  • Unanswered questions
  • Researcher and next verification date

4 · Three struggles

5 · Three questions

  • How do the options compare against essential needs?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Provider Selection helps families selecting a provider or care arrangement complete a care decision record grounded in requirements, preferences, and verified information, without choosing by first impression alone, arguing without agreed comparison criteria, or forgetting unresolved questions once an option feels appealing—even if family members prefer different options.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineHow Do You Compare the Final Care Options?
Primary textA clear comparison does not remove every tradeoff. It helps the family discuss them using the same facts, the person’s preferences, and the requirements care must address. Use the same criteria, resolve key questions, and document the reasons for the decision.
BenefitUse a clearer process for the final care decision.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe Final Care Decision Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Confirm which options are genuinely available for the next arrangement.
  2. Resolve essential capability questions with the provider and relevant professionals.
  3. Record the decision, reasons, and remaining conditions.

Working actions

  1. Choose a manageable set of options that meet the preliminary criteria.
  2. Use consistent questions on tours or provider calls.
  3. Document observations and provider answers separately.
  4. Compare essential care capabilities.
  5. Discuss environment, preferences, and family access.
  6. Invite the loved one’s participation where possible.
  7. Document disagreement without implying a majority vote overrides the person.
  8. Identify the appropriate decision participant or representative for the situation.
  9. Record reasons for the choice or for deferring it.
  10. List any confirmations required before transition.
  11. Identify a backup path when feasible.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The appropriate decision participant has a documented comparison and decision, with remaining conditions and transition actions clearly identified.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Support the active decision
    • Compare current options.
    • Keep unresolved conditions explicit.
    • Move only the agreed decision into transition planning.
  2. Lesson 2 · Prepare the comparison
    • Use the same criteria for each option.
    • Separate essentials from preferences.
    • Avoid a score that hides missing information.
  3. Lesson 3 · Manage the family conversation
    • Let participants explain concerns.
    • Return to the person’s needs and wishes.
    • Distinguish a family contact from decision-making authority.
  4. Lesson 4 · Document the decision
    • Record tradeoffs and outstanding confirmations.
    • Identify the next action.
    • Retain a backup option where feasible.

  • What support should the plan describe?
  • Which instructions are already confirmed?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Personal Care helps families setting up or correcting a current care arrangement prepare a personal care-plan proposal for review with the responsible care professionals, without relying on verbal requests alone, mixing family preferences with treatment orders, or assuming unresolved medication or therapy questions have been addressed—even if care has already started.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineIs the Daily Care Plan Clear Enough to Discuss?
Primary textA family care-plan proposal can make important details easier to discuss: daily assistance, existing instructions, preferences, and questions the clinical team still needs to answer. Bring assessed needs, existing instructions, and unanswered care questions together before the team meeting.
BenefitPrepare a clearer document for the care-plan meeting.
ActionClick below to learn more.
Leads toThe Personal Care Planning Checklist
StatusDraft creative; destination and platform eligibility must be confirmed before publication.

8 · The working checklist

Three priority actions

  1. Collect the current assessment and professional instructions.
  2. Identify questions affecting present daily care.
  3. Prepare a review-ready proposal for the next care-team conversation.

Working actions

  1. Review documented care needs and current instructions.
  2. Organize mobility and transfer assistance information.
  3. Record hygiene and continence support needs.
  4. Document skin-related instructions already provided by professionals.
  5. List nutrition, hydration, and food-texture questions needing confirmation.
  6. Organize current medication-management responsibilities.
  7. Request a full medication review from the appropriate professional where indicated.
  8. Document therapy coordination needs.
  9. Keep preferences separate from clinical instructions.
  10. List questions for Sherene and the responsible care team.
  11. Mark the document as a proposal until relevant care decisions are confirmed.
  12. Record the plan’s author, date, and revision status.

Follow the agreed service scope and professional review routes. Course completion does not certify clinical safety or authorize treatment.

9 · Definition of done

The proposal is complete enough for review, sources and unresolved items are visible, and clinical decisions remain assigned to the appropriate professionals.

10 · Four lessons

  1. Lesson 1 · Prepare for the active care-plan meeting
    • Focus on current support.
    • Bring the latest instructions.
    • Keep the proposal separate from the provider’s authorized plan.
  2. Lesson 2 · Build from assessed needs
    • Use the care requirements brief.
    • Include day-to-day personal assistance.
    • Avoid copying instructions from another person’s plan.
  3. Lesson 3 · Separate orders, preferences, and questions
    • Record existing medication and treatment instructions accurately.
    • Keep family requests distinguishable.
    • Refer prescribing and clinical decisions for appropriate review.
  4. Lesson 4 · Prepare a review-ready plan
    • Identify who needs to confirm each section.
    • Record unresolved items.
    • Version the family proposal before care-team discussion.

  • Assuming activities on a calendar mean the person can attend.

5 · Three questions

  • Which routines matter most now?

  • How do we preserve choice in the daily plan?

6 · Million Dollar Message

Daily Life helps families helping a loved one adjust to a current care arrangement create a good-day plan for care-team discussion that includes preferences, participation support, and personal choice, without assuming activities on a calendar mean the person can attend, leaving meaningful routines out of the care conversation, or turning family preferences into obligations for the person—even if the current routine feels impersonal.

7 · The ad (draft)

HeadlineWhat Would a Good Day Look Like Here?
Primary textA care plan can include more than tasks. Ask how familiar routines, meaningful activities, and relationships can become part of the day—with the person’s preferences at the center. Translate personal preferences into practical questions for the current caregivers.
